manifest.title: One Dip, Many Illusions: The Gap Trap
manifest.subtitle: Synthetic simulation of a single transit event surrounded by large telescope gaps
preparationSteps: Simulated a single transit-like dip at day 115.0 (depth 1.2%, duration 4.5 hours)
Inserted extensive telescope observation gaps (gaps between days 106-113, 117-124, 128-138)

teaching.learningGoal: Discover how a single real dip can fold neatly on multiple arbitrary trial periods when gaps hide missing events.
teaching.skillPracticed: Distinguishing folded alignment from genuine repetition in the time domain
guidedQuestions: If you fold this dataset at P = 3.75 days, the phase plot shows a neat dip at phase 0. Does that mean it repeats every 3.75 days?
Look at the Repetition and Sampling Gaps evidence cards. How many distinct events were actually observed?
Why is checking the time-series chart essential before claiming a periodic exoplanet?
teaching.explanationSummary: Because of telescope gaps, a single dip at day 115 folds into an apparently convincing dip at P = 3.75 days, P = 5.00 days, or other trial periods. However, the Repetition card warns that only 1 single event exists. A single event cannot confirm periodicity without observing subsequent transits.

teacherAnswerReveal.astronomicalContext: Mono-transits occur when only one transit is captured during a mission window.
teacherAnswerReveal.trueNature: Single transient event or long-period candidate (P > 45 days)
teacherAnswerReveal.evidenceEvaluation: The Repetition test reports exactly 1 observed event out of 12 predicted windows. The Sampling Gaps test shows >70% of predicted transit windows were unsampled. Periodicity is unproven.
alternativeExplanations: Long-period exoplanet with P > 45 days whose next transit occurred after observations ended.
Instrumental dropout, cosmic ray hit, or asteroid transit.
